observation: Risko & Gilbert's review frames cognitive offloading as jointly triggered by the objective internal demand a task would impose and a metacognitive estimate of one's own unaided ability; the central open question is what habitual offloading does to underlying cognitive processes, not whether offloading is inherently good or bad.
claim: Offloading is a rational-but-error-prone strategy governed by task demand and (fallible) self-estimation, not an inherently harmful shortcut.
mechanism: Metacognitive monitoring of expected task difficulty and self-capacity gates the decision to offload; this monitoring can be biased.

implications.text: Riemann should not treat offloading of plan/task content as inherently degrading; design around when offloading helps vs. hurts rather than minimizing offloading categorically.

observation: In free-choice reminder-setting experiments, whether a participant sets an external reminder for a future intention tracks their metacognitive confidence in unaided memory, independent of their actual unaided ability.
claim: People's offloading decisions are driven by (fallible) self-belief about memory ability, not by objective ability.
mechanism: unknown - proposed metacognitive monitoring process distinct from ability itself

implications.text: Riemann should not rely on Sam's stated confidence alone to decide whether to offer a reminder/capture prompt; confidence and need for a reminder can diverge.

observation: Participants set more reminders than the objectively optimal strategy would call for ('reminder bias'), occurring in both under-confident and over-confident groups; explicit metacognitive advice about which strategy maximizes performance eliminates the bias.
claim: Over-offloading (not just under-offloading) is a real, common failure mode, and it is correctable with lightweight calibration feedback rather than added friction.
mechanism: Miscalibrated metacognitive evaluation of memory ability, correctable by external accuracy feedback.
context: lab, reminder-setting paradigm with feedback intervention

implications.text: Occasional light-touch calibration nudges ('you don't need to capture this one') may be more valuable than always minimizing capture friction.

observation: Saving an already-studied list of items improves memory for a subsequently studied new list relative to not saving, an effect replicated and extended including when only a subset of items is saved.
claim: Offloading one item frees encoding capacity that is reinvested in learning the next item; offloading is adaptive specifically when new material must still be learned.
mechanism: Reduced rehearsal/maintenance demand on already-saved items frees limited encoding resources, similar to list-method directed forgetting.

implications.text: Offloading a completed or captured plan/task item is beneficial when Sam still has more material to process afterward, since it frees attention for what's next.

observation: Sparrow et al. (2011) reported reduced recall of information expected to remain accessible online, increased recall of its location, and a Stroop-like computer-priming effect after hard trivia questions; the priming component failed a large pre-registered replication (Camerer et al. 2018) and a dedicated 2020 replication, while the core recall-location effect has mixed, generally smaller replications.
claim: The 'Google effect' is a contested, partially-failed-to-replicate finding, not settled science, despite its wide pop-science citation.
mechanism: unknown - original mechanism proposed as reduced encoding effort under expected future access; not established as robust

implications.text: Riemann's design rationale should not cite the Google effect as established justification for limiting offloading; treat as a MYTH-adjacent claim requiring caution.

observation: Offloaded items show a reduced primacy effect but normal recency effect in later free recall (directed-forgetting-like pattern); separately, when a trusted external store is unexpectedly unavailable at test, recall is worse than if the person had relied on internal memory throughout, and people rarely notice when offloaded content has been silently altered.
claim: Offloading content that must later be recalled without the external store is a net memory cost, and losing access to a trusted store unexpectedly leaves you worse off than never having offloaded; people also can't reliably self-monitor for silent corruption of offloaded content.
mechanism: Offloading suppresses rehearsal/encoding of the offloaded item (directed-forgetting-like), and reliance on a store's availability is not error-corrected by the person's own vigilance.

implications.text: FT-offload-store needs an explicit availability/integrity guarantee (visible sync status, no silent data loss/edits) because the failure mode of offloading is not graceful decay but an unnoticed trap.

observation: Offloading working-memory load onto an external tool during a demanding pattern-copying task boosted immediate task performance but reduced later unaided memory for the offloaded material; increasing the effort/cost of offloading reduced how much participants offloaded and improved later retention.
claim: Offloading trades immediate performance for later unaided memory, and the size of that trade-off is tunable via the friction of the offloading action itself.
mechanism: unknown - proposed resource-reallocation away from encoding when offloading is cheap
context: lab, working-memory task with manipulated offloading cost

implications.text: If Riemann ever wants a plan/task item to also be remembered unaided (not the default for plan/execute), a small amount of added friction on offloading could be a tunable design lever.

observation: Adults with ADHD showed a large impairment in time-based prospective memory (remembering to act at a specific clock time with no cue) but little to no impairment in event-based prospective memory (acting when a relevant cue/event occurs), tested within the same sample and paradigm.
claim: ADHD's prospective-memory deficit is specific to time-based intentions, not a general prospective-memory failure; event-based cueing is a relatively spared channel.
mechanism: Time-based PM requires self-initiated clock-monitoring, which depends on sustained attention/executive function disproportionately affected in ADHD; event-based PM is supported by external/environmental cue-triggered retrieval.
population: adults with ADHD (clinical sample vs. matched controls)
context: lab, dissociation paradigm (time-based vs event-based PM within one sample)

implications.text: Convert time-based plan/reminder steps into event-based framing wherever a natural trigger exists (e.g., 'after class' instead of '3pm'); reserve pure time-based alerts for steps with no available cue.

observation: In a randomized controlled crossover trial (N=143, mostly acquired brain injury), a text-paging reminder system (NeuroPage) significantly increased successful completion of individually relevant everyday tasks relative to no-pager baseline (~85% of participants more successful with the pager); follow-up showed some participants retained gains after pager withdrawal (training effect) while others regressed (dependency), tracking severity of executive impairment.
claim: External paging/reminder systems substantially improve real-world task completion in a population with severe memory/planning deficits, but benefit can be either a durable training effect or an ongoing dependency depending on the individual's executive function.
mechanism: External cues substitute for impaired self-initiated retrieval; repeated successful cued completion can, in some but not all users, build habits that persist without the cue.
context: field RCT, real-world everyday task completion

implications.text: Reminder/paging-style features for plan and monitor objectives are well-supported for populations with executive/memory impairment broadly, but transfer to adult ADHD specifically (vs. brain injury) is an open population-transfer question.

observation: Activating an unfinished personal goal produced more self-reported intrusive thoughts, higher accessibility of goal-related words, and worse performance on an unrelated task; forming a specific plan (how, when, where) eliminated these effects, fully statistically mediated by the drop in intrusive thoughts, and the benefit was concentrated in participants who actually went on to execute their plans.
claim: A specific, committed plan relieves the cognitive burden of an unfinished goal by handing control to automatic/environmental triggers; the relief comes from the plan's existence and genuine commitment, not from continuing to hold or rehearse the goal in mind.
mechanism: Implementation-intention formation transfers control of goal pursuit from effortful conscious monitoring to automatic cue-triggered response, resolving the 'uncertainty' that keeps an unfulfilled goal cognitively active.
context: lab, six converging experiments within one paper

implications.text: Riemann's plan-capture flow should force explicit how/when/where specificity and a distinct commitment action, and should not encourage Sam to keep committed plan steps 'in mind' -- offloading fully is the correct default for plan objective.

observation: A theoretical synthesis of situated/embodied/distributed cognition research argues the brain relies on the environment as external memory, an action trigger, and a feedback source, providing cognitive-science grounding for GTD's practice of externalizing commitments ('mind like water'); the authors state explicitly that no controlled empirical study had tested GTD as a complete system, only isolated component practices.
claim: GTD's externalization philosophy has plausible theoretical grounding in distributed cognition but the system itself is empirically unvalidated as a whole; only specific component practices like plan-making (see F21-10) have direct empirical support.
mechanism: Distributed/situated cognition: environment functions as memory store, action trigger, and feedback channel, reducing demand on internal working memory.
population: general adult knowledge workers (theoretical, no primary sample)
context: theoretical synthesis, no controlled trial of GTD as a system

implications.text: Riemann can draw on the externalization philosophy for plan/execute design but should not claim GTD-level validation; rely on component-level evidence (e.g., F21-10) instead of the system-level claim.

observation: Practitioner/applied-ADHD guidance recommends converting time-based reminders into event-based framing, using graduated multi-stage reminders at decreasing intervals before a deadline, and varying reminder content/tone/timing to resist habituation.
claim: Reminder design for ADHD should be event-anchored where possible, staged rather than single-shot, and varied to avoid fading into background noise.
mechanism: unknown - practitioner consensus, plausible given the time-based/event-based PM dissociation (F21-08) but not independently experimentally tested at the format level in adult ADHD

implications.text: Default plan/execute reminders to 2-3 escalating touches with varied phrasing/channel rather than one static alert, as an A/B-testable hypothesis rather than settled design.
